canonical_topic: CO2 Emissions Are an Unavoidable Combustion Byproduct, Varying by Fuel Chemistry
definition: Any carbon-based fuel produces CO2 when fully combusted, and this cannot be engineered away the way carbon monoxide can; the split between CO2 and water output is governed by the fuel's hydrogen-to-carbon ratio and molecular structure.
core_idea: Fuels with more hydrogen relative to carbon, and with small self-contained molecules (like methane/natural gas), produce proportionally more water and less CO2 than fuels with long carbon-carbon-bonded chains or sheets (like coal), which are more carbon-intensive per unit combusted.
key_points: Complete combustion of any carbon-based fuel unavoidably yields CO2 — unlike carbon monoxide, plants cannot design this away.
Methane has the highest hydrogen-to-carbon ratio (4:1) among common fuels, so combustion output skews toward water rather than CO2.
Longer-chain hydrocarbons like coal carry more carbon, so they yield a higher proportion of CO2 relative to water when burned.
Structurally, natural gas is made of small self-contained molecules while coal consists of large sheets of carbon atoms, which is the underlying reason coal is more carbon-intensive than gas.
CO2 emission restrictions are generally treated as a global regulatory issue, in contrast to NOx/SOx/particulates which are handled regionally.
relationships: Contrasts with carbon monoxide, which power plants can largely eliminate via complete combustion.
Contrasts with NOx and SOx, which are regional rather than global regulatory concerns.
trading_implications: Fuel switching between coal and natural gas has a direct, structurally-grounded effect on carbon intensity, which matters for dispatch decisions and cost exposure under carbon-constrained regimes.
caveats: One might assume all fossil fuels emit similar CO2 per unit of energy; the text attributes the difference specifically to hydrogen-to-carbon ratio and molecular structure, not just 'coal is dirtier.'
